    "# Scaling and orientation with `substrata`\n",
    "\n",
    "This tutorial walks through scaling and orienting 3D point clouds with `substrata`. You will load a point cloud, compute or set scale, determine an up vector and depth offset, apply transforms, and visualize results.\n"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 3,
   "id": "fd539a24",
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [],
   "source": [
    "from substrata import *"
   ]
  },

   "id": "206aacdc",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "## Loading a point cloud\n",
    "Substrata lets you load full-size point clouds or stream‑decimate them during load (to reduce memory use and speed up computations when full resolution isn’t required). Often it’s helpful to generate a separate decimated PLY (using `pointclouds.decimate_ply_file()` or the `substrata decimate` CLI). By convention we append the postfix `_dec50M` (for a 50M‑point decimated version) to the original PLY filename."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 4,
   "id": "3603fbbb",
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [
    {
     "name": "stderr",
     "output_type": "stream",
     "text": [
      "Read/Sample: 100%|██████████| 50000000/50000000 [00:02<00:00, 21596716.88vtx/s]\n"
     ]
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "pcd = PointCloud(\"/mnt/sdd/tonga_focal/ton_tof/ton_tof_40m/ton_tof_40m_20241008/ton_tof_40m_20241008_dec50M.ply\",\n",
    "                 max_points=50000000)"
   ]
  },

    "## Scaling the point cloud\n",
    "To scale the point cloud, load marker coordinates for scalebar targets, define the scalebars, compute the scale factor, and apply it as a 4×4 transform."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 6,
   "id": "09c80145",
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [
    {
     "name": "stdout",
     "output_type": "stream",
     "text": [
      "Scalebars(\n",
      "  num_scalebars=4,\n",
      "  scalebar_1='target 31'-'target 33' (0.2m) [partial_coords],\n",
      "  scalebar_2='target 35'-'target 37' (0.2m) [dist=0.1997, residual=-0.0003],\n",
      "  scalebar_3='target 39'-'target 41' (0.2m) [dist=0.2002, residual=+0.0002],\n",
      "  scalebar_4='target 43'-'target 45' (0.2m) [dist=0.2000, residual=+0.0000],\n",
      "  calculated_scalefactor=0.272874,\n",
      "  variance=0.0000000741,\n",
      "  std_error=0.0001571586,\n",
      "  valid_scalebars=3\n",
      ")\n"
     ]
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "# Defining the scalebars\n",
    "SCALEBAR_SIZES_IN_CM = [[\"target 31\", \"target 33\", 0.20],  # top-left\n",
    "                        [\"target 35\", \"target 37\", 0.20],  # bot-left\n",
    "                        [\"target 39\", \"target 41\", 0.20],  # top-right\n",
    "                        [\"target 43\", \"target 45\", 0.20]]  # bot-right\n",
    "\n",
    "# Load the marker coordinates as an Annotations object and then define the scalebars\n",
    "markers = Annotations(\"/mnt/sdd/tonga_focal/ton_tof/ton_tof_40m/ton_tof_40m_20241008/ton_tof_40m_20241008_markers.csv\")\n",
    "scalebars = Scalebars(SCALEBAR_SIZES_IN_CM, markers)\n",
    "print(scalebars)"
   ]

   "source": [
    "## Orientation\n",
    "Depending on your analysis, it’s often useful to orient the point cloud so depth aligns with the z‑axis. You can either (1) directly specify an up vector, or (2) determine the up vector by regressing camera 3D positions against their known depths.\n",
    "\n",
    "For the latter, load camera metadata into a `Cameras` object by providing paths to a `.meta.json` file (generated via the Agisoft Metashape API with camera path/center/transform) and a `.cams.xml` file (exported in Agisoft Metashape using `chunk.exportCameras(\"output_file.cams.xml\")`)."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 9,
   "id": "b78464d8",
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [
    {
     "name": "stdout",
     "output_type": "stream",
     "text": [
      "Cameras(\n",
      "  count=1735, sensors=2, enabled=676,\n",
      "  with_coords=1735, with_datetime=0, with_depth_sensor_m=1059,\n",
      "  world_transform=identity,\n",
      "  groups=['auv_PR', 'photos_PGRAM01'],\n",
      "  groups_counts={'photos_PGRAM01': 676, 'auv_PR': 1059},\n",
      "  coords_bounds=[min=(-18.006, -48.584, -18.032), max=(13.989, 59.819, 19.135), extent=(31.995, 108.402, 37.167)]\n",
      ")\n"
     ]
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "cams = Cameras(\"/mnt/sdd/tonga_focal/ton_tof/ton_tof_40m/ton_tof_40m_20241008/ton_tof_40m_20241008.meta.json\",\n",
    "               \"/mnt/sdd/tonga_focal/ton_tof/ton_tof_40m/ton_tof_40m_20241008/ton_tof_40m_20241008.cams.xml\")\n",
    "print(cams)"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "id": "4ccae2ed",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "If a sufficient number of cameras have measured depth (`depth_sensor_m`, obtained from synchronized sensor data), you can derive the up vector—the 3D direction in the cloud most correlated with depth—and the depth offset (to align the z‑axis approximately with depth) as follows:"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 10,
   "id": "6ca318a3",
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [
    {
     "name": "stdout",
     "output_type": "stream",
     "text": [
      "Found 442 matching cameras/depths for regression\n",
      "  Up vector: [0.008332715344911996, 0.06360581525863027, 0.26619189796023607]\n",
      "  Depth offset: -38.6090 m\n",
      "  Depth per unit: 0.2738 m\n",
      "  Mean squared error: 0.0042 m²\n",
      "  Root mean squared error: 0.0645 m\n",
      "  Mean absolute error: 0.0524 m\n",
      "  R²: 0.9983\n",
      "  Number of matches: 442\n"
     ]
    },
    {
     "data": {
      "image/png": "",
      "text/plain": [
       "<Figure size 1000x500 with 2 Axes>"
      ]
     },
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "display_data"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "up_vector, depth_offset, depth_per_unit, *_ = (cams.get_up_vector_from_camera_depths(plot=True)\n",
    "            )"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "id": "3342237c",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "Apply these parameters to orient the point cloud with `pcd.apply_transform(Transform.from_up_vector(up_vector))` followed by `pcd.apply_transform(Transform.from_depth_offset(depth_offset))`. For convenience, `pcd.apply_orientation_transforms` performs scaling, z‑axis alignment, depth offset, and additional transforms (e.g., aligning the widest dimension to the x‑axis and ensuring +y is upslope).\n",
    "\n",
    "Afterward, plot the different views as a quick check that scaling/orientation were applied correctly."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 11,
   "id": "d22ef47d",
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "image/png": "",
      "text/plain": [
       "<Figure size 800x1200 with 6 Axes>"
      ]
     },
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "display_data"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "pcd.apply_orientation_transforms(scale_factor=1.0,                      # skipping scale as already applied in this case\n",
    "                                 up_vector=up_vector, \n",
    "                                 depth_offset=depth_offset, \n",
    "                                 depth_scale_factor=depth_per_unit)\n",
    "fig = pcd.plot_views()\n",
    "           "
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "id": "a4a636b6",

   "source": [

   "source": [
    " Often `scale_factor` and `depth_per_unit` (scaling along the z‑axis) differ slightly. Applying a global `scale_factor` therefore makes z values only an approximate depth. For absolute depth at a camera, use the `depth_in_m` property. After assigning `up_vector` and `depth_offset` to `Cameras`, you can also plot residuals versus estimated absolute depth."
   ]
